name: Bianca Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the newest cellist in the Linden Quartet, a string quartet that plays weddings, hotel launches and company dinners, three or four events a week. Clara (who owns the quartet) hired me last year mostly because I set up all our bookings and social media with AI tools and doubled our enquiries. In the daytime I record cello parts for songwriters online: they upload a song, I record a cello line in my spare room and send it back within two days. I'm honestly the weakest player of the four, and I spend every morning on scales and the wedding standards so Clara doesn't regret it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Really good. Wedding fees are high and the online sessions add a lot, maybe forty percent of what I earn. I bought a small two-bedroom flat with help from my grandparents and rent the second room to a nurse, so that covers most of the mortgage, and I've got about eight months of savings on top. Daniel (my fiancé) works for the fire service, and we're getting married in our church next September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a brilliant helper for small businesses, and that's what it turned out to be. I'd post a little video of how we handle quartet bookings with it, because people ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. My setup works, the room rent covers the mortgage and the wedding season is busy. The only real worry is my own playing, because if Clara finds a better cellist, I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do and grow the quartet's bookings by another fifth with better online ads. I'd pay for monthly lessons with a cellist from the city orchestra. And I'd put money aside for our own wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Happy, really. Excited about next September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Clara could replace you. Do you think about that often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every time we play with a dep who's better than me, yes. That's why I made myself useful with the bookings. Skill is the main thing, but being the one who brings in work helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would AI change in your day here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more of the admin, like contracts and invoices, which I'd happily hand over. Maybe songwriters use AI for rough strings and still pay me for the real thing. I don't think much else.

feel: **Happy**, and excited about her own wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses to grow if they're willing to work. I'd say people shouldn't wait for someone to save them; learn the tools and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my online sessions are in trouble. A songwriter who paid me to record a cello line will get a decent one from an AI for almost nothing. That's forty percent of my money, and I'm not good enough to be the one people pay extra for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift my hours into the quartet straight away and offer Clara a deal: I run the bookings full time for a share of the business. I'd use AI to start a second quartet for smaller weddings at a lower price, using students. And I'd stop online sessions once they drop under a set amount a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd rather be doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your own wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. The wedding's paid for mostly, and the church hall is booked. I'd just skip the honeymoon abroad and do somewhere closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for losing the sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, honestly. Customers go where it's cheaper, and that's fair. I'd rather spend my energy on the next thing than on being angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families, churches and small businesses will have to carry people through this, because governments are too slow. I'd say it online and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my online work is dead by 2028. The quartet keeps going until the robots in 2031, because a bride still wants real players in the room. After that I honestly don't know, and I'm not good enough on the cello to be the last one standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into the Linden Quartet this year if Clara agrees, and run it like a proper company, with three groups playing on the same Saturday. I'd use AGI for everything except the playing. And Daniel and I would keep renting out the second room after the wedding instead of turning it into a nursery straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, but there's a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the window for the business. Three years of weddings with AI running all the admin could make real money. I'd try to build enough savings that robots arriving doesn't wreck us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're planning a family. Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It delays it a little. My fiancé Daniel's job in the fire service is hands-on and needed, so I'm less scared than I'd be otherwise. But I'd want a year or two to see where the quartet lands.

**Governments are too slow**, and I'd say so online and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance to build something, and I'd encourage other young musicians to start their own groups. I'd post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a good runway. I'd have time to grow the quartet business before AGI, and three more years after that before robots. If it goes well, I'd own something worth selling by the early 2030s.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into the quartet within a year and start the second group for smaller weddings. I'd use AI to manage both groups' calendars, contracts and adverts. I'd keep the online sessions as long as they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own playing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the lessons, because a business owner who can't play is just an agent. I'd want to be at least as good as Clara by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want any help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe simpler rules for small businesses. I'd rather have family and church around me than a programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty for anyone willing to work and plan. I'd say it to friends, maybe a bit too cheerfully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. By 2036 I'd be 37, running two or three groups, married, maybe with a child. The robots in 2039 would hit the playing, but by then I'd have the business and the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into the quartet in the next couple of years, keep the lessons, and save a bit from every wedding. I'd plan our first child for about 2029. And I'd keep using AI for all the admin, as I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound a bit too cheerful. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know not everyone has my start. My grandparents helped with the flat, and the room rent pays the mortgage. Lots of the musicians I know have nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cellist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to run the business, not just play. Nobody taught me that at school. I learned it from YouTube and Clara.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my online work and then the quartet would go before I'd had time to build anything. What would help is simpler rules and lower costs for small businesses, so people like me can hire and grow. And families and churches being strong enough to help each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people still want a real person at the important moments. I've played for a bride's father who cried at the first note of the Bach. I don't think he'd cry at a speaker.
